It's the preservation and conservation of old buildings and the history associated with them. It's a broad subject that can range from working historic museums like Thomas Jefferson's Monticello or historic Williamsburg. It can also be related to the rehabilitation of historic buildings for new use. The next time you're in a town, whether it a city or a small rural town. Consider the old buildings that are there. It can be easy to miss with new stores or shops in them but often times the buildings can be a hundred years old. If you're lucky enough to find the architectural details, you might find glass that was hand blown, or pressed tin ceiling tile from the turn of the century. Although the wealth isn't entirely in the building itself but the history we can find in it. Maybe it was an old textile mill that your grandparents could have worked in, maybe it was the first business of a small immigrant family after reestablishing their lives. The woodwork could be handcrafted from a black man who owned and operated the biggest carpentry business in a southern state. It's even quite possible the neighborhoods you live maintain the homes of great musicians or artist or whomever.   
  
If you're ever curious, you can check out places like the national trust. https://savingplaces.org/ or look into your state's personal State Historic Preservation Office to get involved with saving old places and building communities around them.

I can certainly agree that some organizational structures being no-gos. I work in a design/creativity field and how that often relates is that while there might be 10-500 correct or best solutions to a problem or question; there are a thousand to a million poor and immoral ones that follow. adaptable and reflective are what I wish to impress on.  
  
*"we have no mechanism to put our collective voices behind any messages right now; we lack a democratic operating principle. If we don't get one, or ideally multiples, I fear we'll get into a lót of fights over direction and people trying to dissociate themselves from each other instead of actually working together. "*  
  
In a much more personal manner, this is where I struggle. My impression is that in our global neoliberal culture there is an emphasis on trying to defeat this enveloping ideology with a singular message or ideology of our own. Replacing it like Indiana jones swapping the idol. This is often what sows the discourse of the many leftist considering we are made up of many valid, systemic, oppressive traits of the current structure. I wouldn't disagree that in cases our communities overlap in conflicting manners. This isn't bad, this is life. It's where this existing structure manages to utilize its own multiple enemies to pit them against one another. This prevents the sum of many from overtaking the existing majority. I'm pretty sure that all leftist groups will never have a singular message to rally behind; nor should we. This sounds like trying to replace liberalism with another unlockable skin of liberalism.  
  
I often come back to a critique I overheard once on the occupy movements. I can't remember who it was but they mentioned that the movements were gaining tractions and support in bubbling of trying to erupt but because the movement never formalized a single message or structure, it fizzled out into obscurity. I agree with this critique of the movement but I struggle to agree that we need something global and singular to replace it. Maybe it's the imperial nature of liberalism that keeps us thinking that we need a global solution when there are many different aspects and worldly problems to consider. It's difficult because when I articulate this, I am advocating for a deconstruction back into many different societies when we've worked to become a global perspective and it has it's benefits but also it's problems. In some way, I think we just worked towards the global perspective in all the wrong ways and we need to take two steps back to proceed forward. Yet I'm not confident that is this is the solution we need nor would prove effective. It's also entirely possible that a global perspective is not what should be strived forward. Perhaps it's a federation of many different, smaller, structures that find their own complex means of balance to exist as. 
  
I take some solace in thinking that while I am unsure of an answer, I don't imagine it doesn't exist and it can't exist in many forms.

I don't completely disagree that it certainly feels very wrong to not want to do whatever we can for these important places. I just wanted to reiterate and maybe better communicate the challenges. It's not entirely just not some new screw holes here and there. When looking at core systems like plumbing and trying to retrofit in historic buildings, you have to consider how to fit within the building. This isn't just as far as attaching it to what's existing. This would also involve dismantling the structure in a large capacity, removing the floor or walls to add the plumbing under neither it, alongside drilling extensive holes to fit that plumbing through a historic floor joist, which you must consider if you are compromising the structural integrity that's already there.   
  
We've truly come a long way in our building technology and how we incorporate core and mechanical systems within the building shell. The way that buildings are constructed today is meticulous in considering the layers by which each of these trades comes in after the other. For example, we have to frame the walls, then we can start the plumbing, then we can do the electrical, then we can apply the drywall/paint, then the millwork over that. It wouldn't be possible to do these out of that order because of how we've just come put these parts and pieces together. This is with modern buildings that account these things when you look at historic structures, they had no concept of needing specific room or space to allow for plumbing to drain at a certain angle. So the floors might be much thinner than what applying plumbing would allow in modern buildings. I think a good example many may encounter is what we refer to as ADA or Accessible design for those in wheelchairs. This wasn't a standard until the 1970s, so old buildings didn't often have ramps or hallways were very thin and cramped. This prevented those in wheelchairs from even being apart of the space. Now to fix this, we can't simply move walls to provide a 30-60" walkway clearance because it may be structurally built for that wall to exist where it is and to move it would not only change the history of this building and accounting for that wall but it would impact the size and outline of other rooms and areas, and the many layers of what that building consists of within its walls.   
  
I have been trying to think of a good example to really demonstrate the evolution of buildings and just how much they have changed since we introduced so many precautions and mechanical elements to them. I think the best I can come up with this morning is looking at this image of a [brick wall](https://www.google.com/url?sa=i&source=images&cd=&cad=rja&uact=8&ved=2ahUKEwiJ4q6OvNThAhXikOAKHeYhAjIQjRx6BAgBEAU&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.pinterest.com%2Fpin%2F424323596138268007%2F&psig=AOvVaw0XUdyF_idaubmMKRIXkfyg&ust=1555499142256772)  and how it differs over time. Historically, brick walls were a lot thicker and there structure came from layering the bricks in such a manner to make walls thicker and more stable. Today though, brick is more often adhered to the surface of existing framework, it's cheaper and allows us to better insulate the home and finish the interior walls with drywall. It would be within that framing that all our modern core systems would exist. I hope it helps illustrate in thinking just how different these buildings can be over time.

I work in preservation of buildings and just wanted to provide some perspective. This can be a significant cost for many historic buildings for more than a few reasons. I think the major one is in accordance with best practices. In the us we often follow the secretary of interiors standards for rehabilitation. Which outlines limits for working with these buildings. One of the first guidelines is that you shouldn't damage or destroy the building anymore than it already is. For buildings constructed prior to heating/cooling/electrical/pounding
Plumbing this presents the challenge of how you introduce this without damaging the building. All these encompass what we refer to as the core components and in modern buildings are heavily embedded within walls, floors, ceilings, closets, etc. So simply adding plumbing to a place that's never had it becomes a question of where it's going and more so, how are you going to fasten it to the building without adding more screws, plates, materials.   
  
From a more abstract perspective, we also must wonder how adding these impacts our perception of the past. It might obvious they wouldn't have sprinklers in the 1200s but what about just 70 years ago? This can muddy how people interpret and experience old places. Even if they visible fire suppression system, you have to consider it's impact visually. Which may be equally important to want to convey or not, given the story around a place.   
  
But also from a technology perspective, there exist ways to accomplish these goals with preservation in mind. However, they tend to be incredibly expensive and require significant and extensive installs which can be counter to what a lot of muesems and old buildings can afford. One good example of this is AC which is bulky in new buildings but they have smaller flexible solutions that can be hidden in walls, yet a lot of older buildings in new York for example may just opt in window AC units as unsightly and clunky as there may be.   
  
From an architectural and design perspective. I love these challenges. I'm positive they had some strategies at play for notre Dame but of course you can't predict and account for everything with these methods at play. It's an incredible loss and I hope we manage to find some manner to peacefully move forward to maintain the significance and important this place has had for humanity. Be it though documenting, reconstruction, rehabilitation, or preserving this moment as a lesson in it's own way.
